newsitem.title: USA: Boxing-Tyson's career up in air after license revoked.
newsitem.headline: Boxing-Tyson's career up in air after license revoked.

text.p: Did the Nevada State Athletic Commission deal Mike Tyson a knockout blow?
Some boxing insiders believe the commission's revocation of his boxing license for biting Evander Holyfield's ears during their heavyweight title bout means Tyson is out for the count.

But others feel that Tyson -- the sport's biggest money machine, generating hundreds of millions of dollars over the years -- will return after a year, or may even step into a ring overseas before then.
In the United States, new federal laws governing boxing recommend that a ban such as Nevada's be honored throughout the country, but other states cannot be forced to bar him.
It was considered unlikely Tyson would soon turn up in a ring in Atlantic City, but New Jersey Athletic Commission chief Larry Hazzard suggested Tyson is far from finished.
"Mike Tyson is an integral part of boxing, he's a big name in the sport, so I think Mike needs boxing as much as boxing needs Mike," Hazzard said in a television interview.

The Nevada commission's executive director Marc Ratner acknowledged as much to reporters. "He's the most major draw in the sport," he said after the hearing. "But the sport must continue. You just can't have one fighter have the whole boxing world fall apart."
Even if Tyson, who just turned 31, does come back, he could be past his prime.

Muhammad Ali's legendary trainer Angelo Dundee said the layoff probably meant the end of Tyson's ring career. "I don't think you will see the same Tyson again," he was quoted in the Las Vegas Sun as saying.
Tyson's skills had already declined during the three years he was in prison for a rape conviction, Dundee said.

Tyson himself was not saying anything. He did not attend Wednesday's disciplinary hearing, leaving his lawyers to talk for him. Nevada criminal attorney Oscar Goodman predicted Tyson would be reinstated after a year -- his earliest opportunity to appeal the suspension.
"If he comes back in a year...they're going to say 'look, he did all he could do, he's been punished,'" Goodman told reporters outside the Las Vegas City Hall.
The five-man commission which regulates boxing in Nevada not only revoked Tyson's boxing license, but fined him 10 percent of the $30 million purse he was paid for the June 28 fight with Holyfield.
If Tyson's first request for reinstatement after one year were turned down, he could reapply again every year.
"It could be a lifetime ban, it depends on what the outcome is next year and the year after," said commission member Lorenzo Fertitta.

Nevada's Deputy Attorney General Gordon Fink, who had argued before the commission that Tyson should receive severe punishment, later lambasted the boxer for saying in a public apology last week that when he "snapped" in the ring, it was no different from athletes snapping in other sports.

"Boxing is different from any other sport. To compare it to baseball, football or basketball is meaningless," said Fink. "The object of boxing is violence, and that's why it needs strict adherence to its rules and regulations."
Another commission member, Jim Nave, also noted that under state law, other Nevada boxing license holders risk sanctions if they have any dealings with a banned Tyson.
Asked if that meant Tyson would have to sever ties with promoter Don King, or that co-managers John Horne and Rory Holloway may not manage him while his license is revoked, Nave was circumspect.

"I don't want to get into specific names, but rules are such that anyone who has a license in the state of Nevada, cannot participate in a boxing event with somebody whose license had been suspended or revoked," said Nave.
King, who promoted the Holyfield-Tyson rematch here, was unusually reticent about the case.
But rival promoter Dino Duva said he thought Tyson might try to fight overseas.
"King is supposedly already talking about overseas," Duva told the Reno (Nevada) Gazette Journal. "I hope Tyson and King don't look for a loophole," Duva said.

If Tyson were to fight abroad, he would first have to get permission from his probation officer to travel outside the United States. He still has two years' parole left after serving three years in prison for rape.
If he did get such permission and fight abroad, he would run the risk of alienating the Nevada commission and never receiving reinstatement in his own country.
